title: No Stealing
summary: Prohibits theft of property (and, on one ancient reading, theft of persons — kidnapping, cf. Ex 21:16).
original_audience: Israelite community of smallholders whose animals and tools were survival capital.
immediate_context: Eighth commandment; the Covenant Code's restitution schedule (Ex 22:1-4) supplies the remedies.
historical_context: Where Hammurabi punishes some theft with death (CH 6-10), biblical law is strikingly non-capital about property: thieves pay multiples (double to fivefold restitution), and only manstealing is capital. Property crime never outranks persons — a fact the USofC finds continually inconvenient.
penalty: Restitution: double for possession, four sheep or five oxen for slaughtered/sold animals (Ex 22:1,4); sold into servitude if unable to pay (Ex 22:3).
exceptions: Eating from a neighbor's standing field or vineyard on the spot is lawful (Deut 23:24-25); gleaning rights (Lev 19:9-10) make some 'taking' a right of the poor.
nt_passages: Ephesians 4:28 — 'let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour'
Luke 19:8 — Zacchaeus's fourfold restitution as the Exodus schedule internalized
Acts 4:32-35 — the Jerusalem church holding all things common

internal_contradictions.issue: Is it wrong to steal? The command vs. the Israelites 'borrowing' and despoiling the Egyptians at God's instruction (Ex 3:22, 12:35-36).

usofc_implementation: Theft is handled by the Restitution Administration on the biblical multiplier schedule — no prison for property crime, a genuinely popular reform. Judgment debtors who cannot pay enter covenant labor (see exo-021-002). Gleaning and field-eating rights are codified but hedged: exercising them requires a Gleaner's Card, and the queue for the card is the point.
constitutional_analogue: Replaces incarceration-based larceny law with restitution and debt servitude; collides with the Thirteenth Amendment's exception clause, which the USofC quotes with enthusiasm.
scene_ideas: An RA hearing computing whether a stolen 3D printer is an 'ox' (fivefold, productive capital) or a 'sheep' (fourfold) — the multiplier bar exam question.
A supermarket's legal team arguing shelf-grazing customers are exercising Deut 23:24 field-eating rights.
A Gleaner's Card office that opens for two hours on alternating Tuesdays.
satirical_uses: The despoiling-of-Egypt precedent is taught in USofC law schools as 'the eminent domain of the righteous.'
